teaser: Blindfolded, alone on a globe, with one string left to play. Victorians asked why this was called Hope.
review_notes:
A faint star with rays is visible at the very top of this image (about x 0.37, y 0.02); some sources say the star was dropped from the second (Tate) version, so check the find block against the Tate canvas.
Two versions of 1886: first shown at the Grosvenor Gallery, second given by Watts to the nation in 1897 (Tate). Size about 142 x 112 cm.
Chesterton's remark (1904) that a viewer's first thought would be to call it Despair is paraphrased.
Death of Watts's adopted daughter's baby in 1885 as background; Motto 'I paint ideas, not things' attributed to Watts.
Watts's letter describing the picture is paraphrased, not quoted.
Martin Luther King Jr. sermon 'Shattered Dreams' (1959), Jeremiah Wright sermon (1990), Obama's 2004 speech and 2006 book: verify dates.
Theodore Roosevelt owned a reproduction: verify.

lesson.text: When London first saw this painting in 1886, plenty of visitors thought the label was wrong. A hunched woman, eyes bandaged, alone in a murky nowhere: surely the title should be Despair. The writer G. K. Chesterton later admitted that this would be almost anyone's first thought in front of it.

They had reasons to be confused. For centuries, artists had shown Hope as a calm woman leaning on an anchor, sometimes gazing up at heaven. George Frederic Watts, then 69 and the most respected painter in England, threw the anchor away and kept almost nothing.

What he kept is a figure on a sphere. The sphere is the world, brown and dim, floating in mist. The woman on top of it can't see where she is. And the instrument in her arms, an ancient harp called a lyre, is in very bad shape.

lesson.title: What she still has
lesson.text: Everything that matters happens in the top third of the canvas, around her head.

spots.title: The blindfold
spots.text: A thick white cloth is knotted around her head. She has no view of the world she sits on, and no way to check whether things will get better.

spots.title: Broken strings
spots.text: Pale threads dangle from the top bar of the lyre: strings that have snapped. One single string still runs down, tight, toward her head. It is all she has left to play.

spots.title: Listening
spots.text: She bends her neck until her ear almost rests on the frame, and her fingers reach for the last string. She is straining to catch the faintest sound.

lesson.text: That bent neck changes the meaning of the pose. She is not collapsing. She is concentrating. Watts described the idea in a letter: a figure trying to get all the music she can out of one poor string, listening with all her might.
Watts's Hope is not optimism. It is the decision to keep playing when there is very little evidence that things will turn out well.
The painting came after a family loss. In 1885 the baby daughter of Watts's adopted daughter died at about one year old, and the old painter was deeply shaken. He began Hope soon afterwards.
He did allow one sign that she might be right to keep going. It is easy to miss in the gloom, it takes up almost no room on the canvas, and she herself cannot see it.
Somewhere in the empty sky there is a single point of light. Can you spot it? Search high.

spots.title: The star
spots.text: A tiny star with faint rays, almost at the top edge. It shines behind her, outside her blindfold. Hope, in this picture, does not know that help exists. She plays anyway.

lesson.text: The rest of the surface is a soft haze of blue-green and brown, with no horizon and no sharp line anywhere. Watts dragged and scrubbed his paint so the forms seem to appear through fog. His motto for pictures of this kind was short: “I paint ideas, not things.”

There are two Hopes. Watts painted a first version, then a second one the same year that he liked better. He kept that one out of private hands and gave it to the British nation in 1897. It is the canvas now at Tate Britain.

Cheap prints then carried the image far beyond any gallery. It hung in parlors, schoolrooms and hospital wards across Britain and the United States. President Theodore Roosevelt is said to have owned one.

In 1959 Martin Luther King Jr. described the painting in a sermon about dreams that do not come true. In 1990 a Chicago pastor, Jeremiah Wright, preached on it too. A young man in the congregation named Barack Obama remembered the sermon's phrase about the audacity to hope.

Obama reused that phrase for the speech that made him famous in 2004, and again as the title of his 2006 book, The Audacity of Hope. A blindfolded Victorian figure with one string had reached an American presidential campaign.

quiz.question: Why were early viewers puzzled by the title?
options: The figure looked more like despair than hope
The painting had no figure in it
The title was written in Latin
quiz.explanation: A hunched, blindfolded figure seemed the opposite of hope.

quiz.question: What object did older images of Hope usually include, which Watts removed?
quiz.explanation: Hope was traditionally shown leaning on an anchor.

quiz.question: How many strings of the lyre are still intact?
quiz.explanation: All have snapped except a single string.

quiz.question: What is the only sign of light in the sky?
options: A small star near the top
quiz.explanation: A tiny star shines high up, where she cannot see it.

quiz.question: Which later book title traces back to a sermon about this painting?
quiz.explanation: Obama took the phrase from Jeremiah Wright's sermon on Watts's picture.

facts.text: Watts gave the Tate version of Hope to the British nation himself.
facts.explanation: He donated the second version, the one he preferred, in 1897.

facts.text: The woman in Hope looks up toward the star.
facts.explanation: She is blindfolded and bent over her lyre, with the star behind her.

facts.text: Watts was a young unknown when he painted Hope.
facts.explanation: He was 69 and the most respected painter in England.
